lessons.title: Hello! I am Mira: greetings and ich heiße / ich bin
lessons.goal: Greet people, say goodbye and tell someone your name.

grammar.point: To say your name, use one chunk: Ich heiße … or Ich bin …
grammar.oneLine: Ich heiße Mira. or Ich bin Mira. One verb, never both.

mistake.why: Each chunk already has its verb. Use bin or heiße, not both.

terms.meaning: the word for an action or a state, like come, live or am
I: the word you use for yourself
a group of words you learn as one piece, like a single word
a sentence that tells something and ends with a full stop

cards.title: Before we start: say hello and your name
cards.body: Welcome to German, the start of your course. Chapter 1 is about greeting people, giving your name and saying where you come from, over two study days. A real moment: someone new asks, what is your name? Today you learn your first answer.
steps: You already know: a few words that sound like English, such as Hallo (hello).
New today: two chunks for your name, Ich heiße and Ich bin.
By the end you can: greet someone and say Ich heiße Mira.

examples.why: You already know this: it sounds like English hello, and the order is like English.
New today: Ich heiße + your name. One chunk, one verb.

cards.more: Think of German as a set of building blocks. Some blocks are single words, and some are chunks: groups of words you learn as one brick. Today's big picture: Germans greet people by the time of day, and say their name with one ready-made chunk. Ich heiße Mira means I am called Mira. Ich bin Mira means I am Mira. Pick one brick, and never use both, because each brick already has its own verb. Why does this work? Learning chunks first lets you talk on day one, before the rules. You will learn the rules step by step in the next cards, one small block at a time.

cards.title: Hello: pick by the time of day
cards.body: Germans often greet by the time of day. Guten Morgen in the morning. Guten Tag during the day. Guten Abend in the evening. Hallo works at any time, but it is casual: use it with friends.

examples.why: It is morning, so Guten Morgen.
It is evening, so Guten Abend.
Anna is a friend. Hallo is casual and fits any time.

cards.more: Think of a clock on the wall. Each part of the day has its own greeting. Step 1: look at the time. Step 2: pick the matching one. Guten means good, so Guten Morgen is word for word good morning, just like English. Not sure which to use? Say Hallo. It works all day, but it is casual. Extra example: Guten Morgen, Anna! = Good morning, Anna!

cards.title: Goodbye: a friend or polite?
cards.body: To say goodbye, look at the person. Tschüss is casual: for friends and family. Auf Wiedersehen is polite: for a teacher, a doctor or someone you do not know well.

examples.why: Ben is a friend, so the casual word.
Polite: for people you do not know well.

cards.more: Think of clothes. Tschüss is jeans: relaxed, for friends and family. Auf Wiedersehen is a suit: polite, for a teacher or a doctor. Step 1: who is the person? Step 2: close to you? Say Tschüss. Step 3: not close? Say Auf Wiedersehen. It literally means until we see again. Extra example: Tschüss, Mira! = Bye, Mira!

cards.title: A verb, and your first chunk: Ich heiße
cards.body: A verb is the word for an action or a state, like come, live or am. Every German sentence needs one verb. To say your name, use the chunk Ich heiße + name. It means I am called. Learn it as one piece. Why heiße ends in -e comes in lesson 4.

examples.why: Ich = I. heiße = am called. Then the name.

cards.more: Think of a phone contact card. It has a fixed label: Name: Mira. German does the same. Ich heiße is the label, and you just add your name. Do not take it apart yet. Step 1: say Ich heiße. Step 2: add your name. Done. Why the verb ends in -e is a question for lesson 4. For now it is one block, like a Lego brick you click on. English does this too: you say "How are you?" without thinking about each word. Extra example: Ich heiße Leon. = I am called Leon.

cards.title: The second chunk: Ich bin
cards.body: There is a second way: Ich bin + name. bin means am, so Ich bin Ben is I am Ben. It means the same as Ich heiße Ben. Pick the one you like. Note: ich has a small i unless it starts the sentence.

examples.why: ich comes after Hallo, so it has a small i.

cards.more: Ich bin is a second brick, just like Ich heiße. Think of two doors into the same room. Door one: Ich heiße Ben. Door two: Ich bin Ben. Both lead to I give my name. Pick the door you find easier to say. bin is the German word for am. So Ich bin Anna is word for word I am Anna, just like English. Extra example: Hallo, ich bin Mira. = Hello, I am Mira. Tip: start with Ich bin. It is shorter.

cards.title: One verb only
cards.body: Each chunk already has its verb: heiße or bin. So use one chunk, not both. Ich bin heiße Mira is wrong. It says I am am-called Mira.
cards.more: A sentence is like a car. A car needs one engine. Two engines do not make it faster, they make it break. In German the engine is the verb. Ich heiße already has an engine: heiße. Ich bin has its own: bin. So pick one brick and stop. Ich bin heiße Mira puts two engines in one car. Wrong example in English: I am am called Mira. It sounds odd, right? German feels the same. Right: Ich bin Mira. = I am Mira. Right: Ich heiße Mira. = I am called Mira.

lessons.title: du or Sie? Asking someone's name
lessons.goal: Choose du or Sie and ask for a name in a friendly or a polite way.

grammar.point: Use du with friends and Sie with strangers; each has its own verb form: Wie heißt du? / Wie heißen Sie?
grammar.oneLine: Friend: Wie heißt du? Polite: Wie heißen Sie?

mistake.why: With Sie the verb form is heißen. heißt goes with du.

terms.meaning: a short word that stands for a person, such as ich, du or Sie
friendly and relaxed: how you talk to friends and family
polite: how you talk to strangers, at work and in offices
a word that starts a question, such as wie (how)
a question that starts with a question word; most of them start with W

cards.title: Before we start: friend or polite, and asking a name
cards.body: A real moment: you meet a new neighbour in Germany and want to ask their name. Should you use the friendly word or the polite word? This lesson shows you how to choose, and how to ask both ways.
steps: You already know: Ich heiße … and Ich bin … from lesson 1.
New today: du for friends, Sie for polite talk, and Wie heißt du? or Wie heißen Sie?
By the end you can: ask someone's name in a friendly or a polite way.

examples.en: My name is Mira. And you?
examples.why: You know this: Ich heiße + name, from lesson 1.
New today: with the polite Sie, the verb is heißen.

cards.more: Think of German as having two doors into a conversation: a friendly door (du) and a polite door (Sie). Friends, family and children get du. Adults you do not know, and people at work, get Sie. Why two doors? They show closeness or respect, so you choose the door before you speak. Each door has its own question: Wie heißt du? for a friend, Wie heißen Sie? for someone polite. Step by step: look at the person, choose the door, then use the matching question. The verb changes a little for each door, and you will see the reason in lesson 4. For now, learn both questions as whole chunks.

cards.title: Pronouns: little words for people
cards.body: A pronoun is a short word that stands for a person. ich = I. German has two words for you: du for a friend, Sie for polite talk. You always have to pick one.

examples.why: du: Mira is talking to a friend.

rows: strangers, a teacher, people at work

cards.more: A pronoun is a stand-in. Instead of saying your own name again and again, you say ich. Think of a badge that says me. For the person you talk to, German has two badges. du is the friendly badge. Sie is the polite badge. English has just one word, you, so this part is new. Step 1: look at the person. Step 2: pick du or Sie before you speak. Extra example: Ich bin Leon. Und du? = I am Leon. And you?

cards.title: du or Sie? Look at the person
cards.body: Use du (informal) with friends, family and children. Use Sie (formal) with adults you do not know, at work or in an office. Sie always has a big S. With Sie, people say Herr (Mr) or Frau (Ms) + family name.

examples.why: A friend: first name, casual greeting.

steps: A stranger, or at work? 👉 Sie
Sie + Herr / Frau + family name: Frau Weber, Herr Ali
cards.more: Imagine two outfits. Jeans for friends, a suit for an office. du is the jeans word. Sie is the suit word. Step 1: look at the person. Step 2: friend, family or child? Say du. Step 3: stranger, teacher or boss? Say Sie. If you are unsure, pick Sie. Being too polite is safe. Being too casual can be rude. Sie always has a big S, so you can tell it from other words. Example: Guten Tag, Frau Weber! Wie heißen Sie? = Good day, Ms Weber! What is your name?

cards.title: Ask a friend: Wie heißt du?
cards.body: wie means how. A question that starts with a question word is a W-question. Germans ask: How are you called? Learn Wie heißt du? as a chunk. Answer with Ich heiße … from lesson 1. Und du? asks the same question back.

examples.why: Answer, then ask back with Und du?
Casual greeting, then the du question.

cards.more: Treat Wie heißt du? as one ready-made block, like a sandwich you do not cut open. Word for word it is How are-called you? Step 1: say Wie heißt du? Step 2: wait for the answer. Step 3: ask back with Und du? Why heißt ends in -t comes in lesson 4. Extra example: Hallo! Wie heißt du? – Ich heiße Anna. = Hi! What is your name? – I am Anna.

cards.title: Ask politely: Wie heißen Sie?
cards.body: With Sie the verb changes: heißen, not heißt. The verb form must fit the pronoun. For now, learn the three forms as chunks. Lesson 4 shows the rule behind them.

examples.why: Polite greeting, then the Sie question.
The answer uses a chunk from lesson 1, with first name + family name.

cards.more: Think of a name tag that changes shape for each person. With friends the tag says heißt. With Sie the tag says heißen. You do not build them yet. You just match them like keys to locks. du fits heißt. Sie fits heißen. Step 1: choose du or Sie. Step 2: take the matching verb. Lesson 4 shows the pattern, so for now, copy it. Extra example: Wie heißen Sie? = What is your name? (polite). Wie heißt du? = What is your name? (friend).

cards.title: The verb comes right after wie
cards.body: Look at the order in a W-question: question word first, verb second, person third. Wie heißt du? is right. Wie du heißt? is wrong.

examples.why: wie, then the verb, then du.
wie, then the verb, then Sie.
The verb must come right after wie.

cards.more: Picture a train with cars in a fixed order. Car 1: the question word. Car 2: the verb. Car 3: the person. German never swaps the cars. Wie heißt du? has wie first, heißt second, du third. Wie du heißt? puts du in the verb's seat. The train will not leave. English is different: you can say You are called what? as a joke, but a real question flips the order. Extra example: Wie heißen Sie? = Wie, then heißen, then Sie. Easy.

cards.title: How are you? Wie geht's?
cards.body: Wie geht's? means How are you? It is casual, so use it with du people. A good answer is Gut, danke! (Good, thanks!). Learn both as chunks. und means and.

examples.why: A casual question for a friend.

cards.more: Wie geht's? is a small ritual, like a wave of the hand. Word for word it is How goes it? English does the same: How's it going? Step 1: ask Wie geht's? Step 2: answer Gut, danke! Step 3: ask back with Und du? Learn each as a block. Extra example: Gut, danke! Und du? = Good, thanks! And you?

lessons.title: Where from, where you live: the verb in second place
lessons.goal: Ask and say where you come from and where you live, with the verb in the right place.

grammar.point: The verb is always the second part: in statements and in W-questions
grammar.oneLine: Ich komme aus Wien. Woher kommst du? The verb is part 2.

mistake.why: In a W-question the verb comes right after the question word.

terms.meaning: the part that says who the sentence is about: ich, du, Sie, Ben
the place of a part in the sentence: first, second, third
a sentence that tells something and ends with a full stop
the word that opens a W-question: woher (where from), wo (where), wie (how)

cards.title: Before we start: where you come from and live
cards.body: A real moment: at a language café someone asks, Woher kommst du? Where are you from? Today you learn to say where you come from and where you live. There is one big rule: the verb always sits in part 2.
steps: You already know: Ich bin + name, and Wie heißt du?
New today: Ich komme aus … and Ich wohne in …, with the verb in part 2.
By the end you can: say where you come from and live, and ask Woher kommst du?

examples.why: You know this: ich bin from lesson 1.
New today: wohnen (to live) with in + place. The verb is part 2.

cards.more: Think of a sentence as a row of seats. Seat 1 is who or what, seat 2 is the verb, and the rest comes after. German keeps the verb in seat 2, like a fixed chair at a table. Ich komme aus Wien: the verb komme sits in seat 2, then the place. Woher kommst du? keeps the verb in seat 2 too, after the question word. Why does German do this? One fixed seat means you always know where to look for the verb. Step by step: find the verb, put it in seat 2, then build the rest around it. The next cards practise each seat.

cards.title: Count parts, not words
cards.body: A sentence is made of parts. A part is one word or a few words that belong together. Mira Bauer is one part. The subject is the part that says who: ich, du, Sie, Ben.
cards.more: Think of a sentence as a train. A part is one train car. A car can hold one word, or a few words that travel together. Anna Weber is two words but one car, because it is one name. Step 1: read the sentence. Step 2: ask who? That car is the subject. Step 3: count the cars. Extra example: Ich heiße Anna Weber. = Ich | heiße | Anna Weber. Three parts, four words.

cards.title: Where you come from: Ich komme aus …
cards.body: kommen means to come. Ich komme aus + a country or a city = I come from. aus means from, and aus + the place is one part. Learn Ich komme aus as a chunk.
cards.more: Ich komme aus is a ready-made block with a gap, like a sticker that says I come from ___. Step 1: say Ich komme aus. Step 2: fill the gap with a country or a city. aus + the place stick together as one part. The order is the same as in English. Extra example: Ich komme aus Italien. = I come from Italy.

cards.title: Where you live: Ich wohne in …
cards.body: wohnen means to live, in a place. Ich wohne in + a city or a country = I live in. Learn Ich wohne in as a chunk.
cards.more: Ich wohne in is a block with a gap too: I live in ___. Think of a pin on a map. Step 1: say Ich wohne in. Step 2: add the place. Do not mix them up: aus is where you started, in is where you are now. Extra example: Ich wohne in Wien. = I live in Vienna.

cards.title: The big rule: the verb is part 2
cards.body: A statement is a sentence that tells something. It ends with a full stop. Position means the place of a part: first, second, third. In a German statement the verb is always in position 2.
cards.more: Imagine seats on a bus with numbered seats. Seat 2 belongs to the verb. Always. Who sits in seat 1 can change, but the verb stays in seat 2. Step 1: count the parts. Step 2: put the verb in seat 2. Ich wohne in Berlin: Ich is seat 1, wohne is seat 2, in Berlin is seat 3 (it counts as one part). Now put In Berlin in seat 1: In Berlin wohne ich. The verb still sits in seat 2. English moves the verb around freely. German keeps it fixed. Extra example: Aus Wien komme ich. = From Vienna I come (I come from Vienna).

cards.title: Question words: woher and wo
cards.body: woher means where from. wo means where. Answer woher with aus. Answer wo with in.

examples.why: woher gets an answer with aus.
wo gets an answer with in.

cards.more: Think of two arrows. woher points back to where you started, and the answer uses aus. wo is a pin on the map where you are now, and the answer uses in. Step 1: look at the question word. Step 2: woher means aus, wo means in. Both start with wo, which sounds like where. Extra example: Woher? – Aus Wien. Wo? – In Hamburg. = Where from? – From Vienna. Where? – In Hamburg.

cards.title: W-questions: the verb is part 2 too
cards.body: In a W-question the question word is part 1. The verb is part 2. The person comes after the verb. Woher kommst du? is right. Woher du kommst? is wrong.

examples.why: The verb must come right after woher.

cards.more: Same bus, same seats. In a W-question the question word takes seat 1. The verb stays in seat 2. The person gets seat 3. Woher kommst du? has woher first, kommst second, du third. The verb never moves out of seat 2. Wrong: Woher du kommst? Here du sits in seat 2. The verb loses its seat. Extra example: Wo wohnen Sie? = Where do you live? (polite). Step: question word, verb, person. Say it three times out loud.

cards.title: Forms for du and Sie
cards.body: Like heißen, these verbs change with the person. Learn these forms as chunks for now. Lesson 4 shows the pattern behind them.
cards.more: Think of verbs as clothes that change for each person. Today you only copy them, like copying a phone number. du gets one ending, Sie gets another. Do not worry about why. Lesson 4 explains the pattern. Copy now: du kommst, Sie kommen. du wohnst, Sie wohnen. Extra example: Woher kommen Sie? = Where do you come from? (polite). Wo wohnst du? = Where do you live? (friend). Match: du with -st, Sie with -en.

lessons.title: Verb endings: ich -e, du -st, er/sie -t, Sie -en
lessons.goal: Change the verbs kommen, wohnen and heißen to fit ich, du, er, sie and Sie.

grammar.point: A regular verb drops -en and takes the ending that matches the subject
grammar.oneLine: Take off -en and add: ich -e, du -st, er/sie -t, Sie -en.

mistake.why: The ending -e belongs only to ich. er, sie and names take -t.

terms.meaning: the dictionary form of a verb; it ends in -en, like kommen
what is left when you take -en off the infinitive: komm- from kommen
the small piece glued to the stem; it changes with the person
to give a verb the ending that fits the subject
er = he, sie (small s) = she

cards.title: Before we start: verb endings
cards.body: A real moment: a friend asks where Mira lives, and you need to talk about yourself and about her. Verbs change their ending to match who is doing the action. Today you learn the four endings and how to find the right one in three steps.
steps: You already know: ich komme, ich wohne and du heißt from lessons 1 to 3.
New today: the endings -e, -st, -t and -en added to the stem.
By the end you can: change kommen and wohnen for ich, du, er, sie and Sie.

examples.why: You know this: ich komme from lesson 3.
New today: du takes -st, so wohnen becomes wohnst.

cards.more: Think of a verb as a word with a body and a coat. The stem is the body: komm-, wohn-. The ending is the coat you put on, and it must fit the person. Ich gets -e, du gets -st, er and sie get -t, and Sie gets -en. Why? Each person needs a different coat, so the listener knows who is doing the action, even without the name. Step by step: take off -en from the dictionary form to find the stem, keep the stem the same, then add the coat for the person. The next cards show the coats in a table, and then let you practise them.

cards.title: The infinitive and the stem
cards.body: The infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb. It ends in -en: kommen, wohnen. Take off -en and you get the stem: komm-, wohn-. The stem stays the same. Only the end changes.
cards.more: Think of a verb as a tree: the stem is the trunk and the ending is a branch. The trunk stays. Only the branch changes. kommen has the trunk komm- and the branch -en. Step 1: find the -en at the end of the dictionary word. Step 2: cut it off. Step 3: what is left is the stem. kommen without -en is komm-. wohnen without -en is wohn-. Why German does it: the trunk carries the meaning, the branch tells who. Extra example: sagen (to say) gives sag-.

cards.title: Stem + ending
cards.body: An ending is the small piece you glue to the stem. It must fit the person. Now you see why it is ich komme but du kommst. Giving a verb its ending is called conjugating.
cards.more: Picture a Lego brick (the stem) and a small clip (the ending). Same brick, different clips for different people. Step 1: pick the stem, like wohn-. Step 2: ask who is it. Step 3: clip on the matching ending. ich gets -e, du gets -st, Sie gets -en. So: ich wohne, du wohnst, Sie wohnen. Why German does it: the clip tells you who is acting, so German can be short. Extra example: komm- + st = kommst. Du kommst aus Italien. = You come from Italy.

cards.title: er and sie: he and she
cards.body: er means he. sie with a small s means she. Both take the ending -t. A name works the same way: Ben = er, Mira = sie. The verb is still part 2.

examples.de: Ben wohnt in Hamburg, aber er kommt aus Spanien.
examples.en: Ben lives in Hamburg, but he comes from Spain.
examples.why: Ben = er, so -t twice. aber = but.

cards.more: Every person has a stand-in word. Ben is a he, so er. Mira is a she, so sie. Both take -t, like one key for two doors. Step 1: who is it? Step 2: he or she? Step 3: stem + t. kommen: komm + t = kommt. A name does the same job as er or sie. Later you will meet another sie, but not yet. Extra example: Sie wohnt in Berlin. = She lives in Berlin.

cards.title: sie or Sie? Look at the ending
cards.body: Small sie (she) takes -t: sie wohnt. Big Sie (polite you) takes -en: Sie wohnen. At the start of a sentence both have a big S. Then the ending tells you who it is.

examples.why: -en, so it is the polite you.

examples.en: Where do you live, Ms Weber?

cards.more: Two words sound the same, but they wear different shoes. Small sie (she) wears -t. Big Sie (polite you) wears -en. Look at the shoes, the verb ending. Sie kommt aus Spanien: -t means she. Sie kommen aus Spanien: -en means you, polite. Why German works this way: at the start of a sentence both start with a big S, so the verb ending is your only clue. Step 1: look at the verb ending. Step 2: -t means she, -en means polite you. Extra example: Sie wohnt in Wien. = She lives in Vienna.

cards.title: heißen: one small change
cards.body: The stem of heißen is heiß-. The letter ß is a sharp s sound, so the stem already ends in s. That is why du gets only -t: du heißt, not du heißst. er and sie get heißt too.

examples.why: heiß + t: the s-sound is already there.

cards.more: Think of a snake that already has an s at the end. The stem heiß- ends in the sharp s sound. The du ending -st also has an s. So heiß + st would give a double s sound: heißst. German skips one s, so du gets only -t. Step 1: stem heiß-. Step 2: du ending would be -st. Step 3: the s is already there, so just add -t. Result: du heißt. Extra example: Du heißt Ben. = Your name is Ben. This is the only odd one so far. er and sie also say heißt.

cards.title: Find the form in 3 steps
cards.body: To find the right form, ask: Who is the subject? Which ending goes with that person? Then glue the ending to the stem.

examples.why: Anna = sie → -t → wohnt. auch = too, hier = here.

cards.more: Think of a recipe with three steps. Step 1: who is the subject? Step 2: which ending fits that person? Step 3: glue it onto the stem. Example: Who? du. Ending? -st. Stem? komm-. Result: kommst. Do the same every time and you cannot go wrong. A recipe works because you do not have to think, you just follow. Extra example: Who? er. Ending? -t. Stem wohn-. Result: er wohnt. Er wohnt in Berlin. = He lives in Berlin.

lessons.title: sein: bin, bist, ist, sind, and introducing others
lessons.goal: Use the verb sein and introduce other people with Das ist.

grammar.point: sein is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, Sie sind
grammar.oneLine: sein breaks the stem + ending pattern, so learn bin, bist, ist, sind by heart.

mistake.why: bin belongs only to ich. The du form of sein is bist.

terms.meaning: a verb that does not follow the stem + ending pattern, so you learn its forms by heart
to tell someone who another person is
this or that: Das ist Ben. = This is Ben.
who: the question word for people

cards.title: Before we start: sein and introducing people
cards.body: A real moment: a friend shows you a photo and says, Das ist Anna. This is Anna. Today you learn sein (to be), the most important verb in German. You will use it to introduce people and to say what they do for work.
steps: You already know: ich bin from lesson 1, and the endings -st and -t from lesson 4.
New today: sein has its own forms (du bist, er ist, Sie sind) and Das ist …
By the end you can: introduce someone with Das ist and say Ben ist Student.

examples.why: You know this: ich bin from lesson 1.
New today: Das ist + name introduces someone.

cards.more: Think of sein as the odd one out in a class. Most verbs follow the coat rule from lesson 4, but sein has its own forms, like a friend who dresses differently. Big picture: sein means to be. You use it to say who you are, who someone else is, and what someone is like. Das ist means this is, and Wer ist das? means who is that? Jobs have no word for a in German, so you say Ben ist Student. Why? German treats a job like a description, not a thing. You will learn the forms by heart, one small group at a time, in the next cards.

cards.title: sein: a verb that breaks the pattern
cards.body: An irregular verb does not follow the stem + ending pattern from lesson 4. sein (to be) is the most important one. You know ich bin already. The other forms look different, so learn them by heart.
cards.more: Think of a stubborn friend who always has his own special seat. Most verbs follow the stem + ending recipe. sein does not. It is like a person whose name changes each time you meet them: ich bin, du bist, er ist, Sie sind. You cannot build them. You just know them, like your phone number. Why? sein is used so often that it kept its old forms through history. Tip: say the four forms out loud each day for a week. Extra example: Du bist nett. = You are nice.

cards.title: Still part 2
cards.body: Each person has its own form of sein: du bist, er ist, Sie sind. Never build it from a stem: there is no du seinst. The verb is still in position 2.
cards.more: Think of sein as a coat rack with a hook for each person. Each hook holds one form: bin for ich, bist for du, ist for er and sie, sind for Sie. A hook cannot be built from a stem. There is no du seinst. If you say it, a German will smile. The verb still sits in seat 2. Step 1: who is it? Step 2: grab the matching form. Extra example: Er ist neu. = He is new. Sie sind Frau Weber. = You are Ms Weber.

cards.title: Who is that? Das ist …
cards.body: To introduce someone, say Das ist + name. das means this or that. To ask, say Wer ist das? wer means who. das takes ist, like er and sie.

examples.de: Wer ist das? – Das ist Anna.
examples.en: Who is that? – That is Anna.
examples.why: Question with wer, answer with Das ist.

examples.de: Das ist Ben. Er kommt aus Spanien.
examples.en: This is Ben. He comes from Spain.
examples.why: Introduce, then say more with er.

cards.more: Das ist + name is like pointing a finger and saying: this is ... Step 1: point at the person. Step 2: say Das ist. Step 3: add the name. To ask, swap it: Wer ist das? means who is that? das is the same word in the question and the answer. ist is still part 2. Extra example: Das ist Ben. = This is Ben.

cards.title: Jobs: no word for 'a'
cards.body: To say what someone does, use sein + the job. German uses no word for 'a' here. Ben ist Student. = Ben is a student.
cards.more: English says a student, a teacher. German drops the a when you say what someone does for a living. It is like a name tag: you just write the job. Step 1: sein form. Step 2: the job word. Ben ist Student. Frau Weber ist Lehrerin. No ein, no a. Why German does it: a job is seen as what someone is, like a label, not one of many students. Extra example: Ich bin Lehrer. = I am a teacher.

cards.title: -in: the word for a woman
cards.body: Many job words have two forms. For a man: Lehrer, Student. For a woman, add -in: Lehrerin, Studentin.

examples.why: Mira is a woman: Student + in.

cards.more: Think of a job word as a badge. The basic badge is for a man. To show a woman, stick a small -in on the end, like adding a sticker. Lehrer + in = Lehrerin. Student + in = Studentin. Step 1: start with the man word. Step 2: add -in for a woman. Why German does it: it shows right in the word who is meant. Extra example: Leon ist Lehrer. = Leon is a teacher. Anna ist Lehrerin. = Anna is a teacher.

cards.title: Say what someone is like
cards.body: After a form of sein you can also say what someone is like: nett (nice), neu (new), super (great).
cards.more: A describing word is like a sticker on a name tag. It says what someone is like. Step 1: say who. Step 2: say the right form of sein: bin, bist, ist or sind. Step 3: stick on the word: nett, neu or super. These words stay the same here. Extra example: Du bist nett. = You are nice.

lessons.title: Spelling, languages and two kinds of questions
lessons.goal: Spell words, talk about languages and ask both W-questions and yes/no questions.

grammar.point: A W-question has the verb in position 2; a yes/no question starts with the verb
grammar.oneLine: Question word + verb for W-questions, verb first for yes/no questions.

mistake.why: Two things: the question starts with the verb, and with du the e of sprechen becomes i. (In fast speech you will also hear Du sprichst Englisch? with a rising voice. That is fine to hear, but write and learn verb first.)

terms.meaning: the two dots over a, o or u: ä, ö, ü
the letter ß; it sounds like ss
to say a word letter by letter
when the vowel inside the stem changes, like e → i in sprechen
a question you answer with ja (yes) or nein (no); it has no question word, and the verb comes first

cards.title: Before we start: languages and yes or no questions
cards.body: A real moment: someone asks, Sprichst du Deutsch? Do you speak German? You may also need to spell your name letter by letter. Today you learn the extra letters, language names, and yes or no questions, where the verb comes first.
steps: You already know: W-questions with the verb in part 2, such as Woher kommst du?
New today: spelling, language names, and yes/no questions with the verb first.
By the end you can: spell your name and ask Sprichst du Englisch?

examples.why: You know this: a W-question, with the verb in part 2.
New today: a yes/no question has no question word. The verb comes first.

cards.more: Think of a question as a door you open. A W-question has a signpost at the front, a word like wo or woher. A yes/no question has no signpost: you just move the verb to the front. Why? In German, the moved verb is the switch that turns a statement into a question. Step by step: say the statement, move the verb to the front, then answer ja or nein. English adds do or does, but German only moves the verb. Spelling uses a similar idea: say the letters one by one. The next cards show each step.

cards.title: Four extra letters
cards.body: German has the same 26 letters as English, plus four. An umlaut is the two dots over a vowel: ä, ö, ü. The two dots change the sound. The sharp s, ß, sounds like ss. You know some already: Österreich, Tschüss, heißen.

examples.why: ö: say 'ay' as in 'say', but round your lips. (Close to 'ur' in 'fur', without the r.)
ü: say 'ee' as in 'see', but round your lips as if whistling.

cards.more: Think of the alphabet as a piano with four extra keys. The dots on ä, ö, ü are like a little hat that changes the sound, so they are not the same letter as a, o, u. And ß is a special key that sounds like a double s. Step 1: see two dots. Step 2: say the new sound, not the old one. Why they exist: German used to write a small e above the letter, and over time it became two dots. Extra example: heißen sounds like hy-ssen. Tschüss = goodbye (casual).

cards.title: Spelling: Wie schreibt man das?
cards.body: To spell means to say a word letter by letter. To ask for it, say Wie schreibt man das? (How do you write that?). Learn it as a chunk. Then say the letters one by one.
cards.more: Spelling is saying letters one by one, like beads on a string. Wie schreibt man das? is one block. Word for word it is How writes one that? Step 1: ask the block. Step 2: listen to the letters. Step 3: write them down. Extra example: Wie schreibt man das? – M – I – R – A. = How do you spell that? – M-I-R-A.

cards.title: Languages often end in -isch
cards.body: Many languages end in -isch: Spanisch, Italienisch, Englisch. German is Deutsch. In Austria people speak Deutsch too. Language names start with a big letter.
cards.more: Many language names share a tail: -isch. English does too: Spanisch is Spanish, Englisch is English. Step 1: think of the country. Step 2: change the end to -isch. Deutsch is the odd one out, so learn it by itself. Always write language names with a big letter. Extra example: Italien → Italienisch = Italy → Italian.

cards.title: sprechen: the e becomes i
cards.body: sprechen means to speak. It takes the normal endings. But for du and er/sie, the e in the stem changes to i. This is a stem change. ich and Sie keep the e.
cards.more: Think of the stem as a trunk that sometimes bends in the middle. For sprechen, the e in spr-e-ch bends to i, but only for du and er/sie. Step 1: ich spreche (normal). Step 2: du sprichst (e becomes i). Step 3: er spricht (e becomes i). Step 4: Sie sprechen (normal again). Why it happens: it is an old sound change that stuck. Do not try to build it, just learn this one. Extra example: Anna spricht Spanisch. = Anna speaks Spanish.

cards.title: A little: ein bisschen
cards.body: To say you speak a little, put ein bisschen before the language. ein bisschen and the language are one part, after the verb.
cards.more: ein bisschen is a pinch, like a pinch of salt. It makes the language smaller: a little. Step 1: say Ich spreche. Step 2: add ein bisschen. Step 3: add the language. The pinch and the language together are one part. Extra example: Ich spreche ein bisschen Englisch. = I speak a little English.

cards.title: Yes/no questions: the verb goes first
cards.body: A yes/no question is one you answer with ja (yes) or nein (no). It has no question word. The verb moves to position 1, and the person comes right after it. The verb form stays the same.

examples.en: Does Anna live in Vienna? – Yes.

cards.more: Think of a question as a flipped sentence. Normal: Du wohnst in Berlin. For a yes/no question, flip the verb to the front: Wohnst du in Berlin? Step 1: write the statement. Step 2: move the verb to position 1. Step 3: the person comes right after it. The verb stays the same. English adds do or does (Do you live in Berlin?). German skips that and just moves the verb. Extra example: Bist du Mira? = Are you Mira? Answer: Ja or Nein.

cards.title: Two kinds of questions
cards.body: W-question: question word in position 1, verb in position 2. Yes/no question: verb in position 1. English adds do or does. German just moves the verb.

examples.why: yes/no question with sein: bist first.

cards.more: Think of two kinds of questions as two doors. Door one: you want information, so start with a question word (W-question). The verb comes second. Door two: you want ja or nein, so start with the verb. Step 1: do I want a detail or a yes/no? Step 2: pick the door. Wo wohnst du? asks for a place. Wohnst du in Berlin? asks yes or no. Extra example: Woher kommen Sie? is door one. Kommen Sie aus Spanien? is door two.

reading.text:

listening.title: Wie schreibt man das?
listening.script:
Frau Weber: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie?
Leon: Guten Tag. Ich heiße Leon Rossi.
Frau Weber: Rossi? Wie schreibt man das?
Leon: R – O – S – S – I.
Frau Weber: Danke. Woher kommen Sie, Herr Rossi?
Leon: Ich komme aus Italien. Ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
Frau Weber: Sprechen Sie Englisch?
Leon: Ja. Und ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.
Frau Weber: Super! Das ist Anna. Sie wohnt auch in Berlin.
Anna: Hallo, Leon! Wie geht's?
Leon: Gut, danke! Sprichst du Italienisch?
Anna: Nein. Ich spreche Deutsch und Spanisch.
